messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Vignette:
Caleb Morrison is a 26-year-old detective, married, who presented for intake following what he described as nearly two years of "not being able to get my head straight." He is soft-spoken in session, choosing his words carefully, and carries himself with the practiced composure of someone accustomed to concealing internal states. His PCL-5 score of 72 places him in a range of severe posttraumatic symptomatology, and the clinical picture that emerged across the first several sessions is one of a man whose professional identity and personal life have been quietly dismantled from the inside.

Approximately eighteen months ago, Caleb ended a relationship with a woman he had been with for nearly three years before his current marriage. He had never disclosed the relationship to colleagues or family in full, and what he disclosed in session came haltingly. His former partner's abuse had been physical and had escalated over the final year they were together. On the night that crystallized his trauma, she had been drinking heavily — the smell of alcohol sharp and close — and had struck him repeatedly, leaving visible bruising across his ribs and jaw. He remembered the particular sound of her voice during it: a low, flat tone that bore no resemblance to anger, which he found more frightening than shouting would have been. He left that night and did not return, but he has never fully left the room.

In the months that followed, Caleb found that certain things pulled him back without warning. The smell of alcohol — encountered at crime scenes, at department gatherings, even on the breath of a witness he was interviewing — could collapse the distance between then and now entirely. The memory would arrive with the same flat voice, the same specific quality of helplessness, complete and unbidden. He describes the memories as arriving fully formed, with a clarity he finds almost insulting — not blurred or partial but precise, as though the event had been rendered in high definition while the rest of his life had grown dim. He sometimes hears things during these intrusions: her voice, a particular phrase she used. When visible injuries appear in his work — and they appear often; he is a detective — something in his stomach turns before his mind has caught up, and the nausea that follows is not metaphorical. It is physical, immediate, and humiliating to him in a professional context.

What Caleb has come to believe about himself and the world has shifted in ways he finds difficult to articulate but impossible to ignore. He had always thought of himself as someone who read people accurately — it was, he felt, the core of what made him good at his job. Now he was certain that this capacity had been an illusion. People were not what they seemed; he had lived inside that proof. He felt permanently outside something he could not name — not quite belonging to his colleagues, his marriage, or any ordinary version of adult life. His faith, which had been quiet but present, had not survived the realization that he had been harmed by someone he had trusted completely.

His marriage has borne the weight of much of this. Caleb avoids being touched — not dramatically, but consistently, with small deflections and repositioning that his wife has noticed and named. He does not explain it to her. He numbs what he feels in her presence as much as anywhere else, and he is aware that she experiences this as withdrawal rather than protection. He has also stopped allowing himself to relax, even at home, even when nothing is wrong; stillness feels to him like a posture he can no longer afford. The consequence has been a marriage that is technically intact but functionally hollowed out, and it was his wife's quiet statement that she felt she was living with a stranger that finally brought him to seek help.

What Caleb is most afraid of, he said at the end of the intake session, is that she is right.
